lead: Ion exchange swaps ions between a solution and a solid resin. The resin carries fixed charged groups balanced by loosely held counter-ions; ions from the water take their place and the counter-ions go into the water, equivalent for equivalent. A water softener swaps calcium and magnesium for sodium; a demineraliser swaps every cation for H<sup>+</sup> and every anion for OH<sup>−</sup>, which combine to water. Columns of resin run through a cycle of service and regeneration, much like a fixed-bed adsorber.
prereq: The column behaviour follows Batch and fixed-bed adsorption: breakthrough curves.

blocks.text: Most resins are beads of polystyrene cross-linked with divinylbenzene (about 8 %) and carrying ionic groups throughout the bead, not just on its outside. The groups decide the type:

head: Resin
Fixed group
Regenerated with
Note
rows: NaCl (Na form) or HCl, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (H form)

blocks.text: Softening on a sodium-form strong acid resin is 2R–SO<sub>3</sub>Na + Ca<sup>2+</sup> ⇌ (R–SO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Ca + 2Na<sup>+</sup>. Charge is conserved, so one Ca<sup>2+</sup> releases two Na<sup>+</sup>: the number of ions in the water rises but the equivalents do not change. That is why ion-exchange quantities are counted in equivalents (eq, or meq = eq/1000), the moles of charge, and hardness is often quoted as mg/L of CaCO<sub>3</sub> (50.0 mg per meq). The reaction is reversible, which is what lets a strong brine push the calcium back off.

Total capacity is the number of exchange groups: about 4.5–5 eq per kg of dry strong acid resin, or 1.8–2.0 eq per litre of wet settled bed. Operating capacity is what a column actually delivers between regenerations, usually 0.8–1.4 eq/L, because the bed is switched at breakthrough and regeneration is never complete.

A resin prefers some ions over others. In dilute solution the rules are: higher charge wins, and among equal charges the ion with the smaller hydrated size (larger atomic number in a group) wins. For a strong acid resin: Ba<sup>2+</sup> > Pb<sup>2+</sup> > Ca<sup>2+</sup> > Mg<sup>2+</sup> > K<sup>+</sup> > NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> > Na<sup>+</sup> > H<sup>+</sup>. For a strong base resin: SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> > NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> > Cl<sup>−</sup> > HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> > OH<sup>−</sup>. Selectivity is put as a number by the selectivity coefficient K<sub>A/B</sub> = (y<sub>A</sub>x<sub>B</sub>)/(x<sub>A</sub>y<sub>B</sub>) for two ions of equal charge, with y the fraction on the resin and x in the solution.

So calcium is held in preference to sodium in a softener, yet a 10 % brine, with sodium hundreds of times more concentrated, drives it off: concentration overcomes selectivity during regeneration. In concentrated solution the preference for divalent ions also weakens, which helps.

items: Service: raw water flows down through the bed; an exchange zone moves down as in a fixed-bed adsorber, and the run stops when the outlet hardness or conductivity rises.
Backwash: water flows up to expand the bed, lift out trapped dirt and regrade the beads.
Regeneration: regenerant (8–12 % NaCl, 4–6 % HCl or 2–4 % NaOH) passes slowly through the bed; more than the stoichiometric amount is needed, often two to three times, to push the reaction back.
Rinse: water washes out the excess regenerant before the next service run.

blocks.text: In co-current regeneration the regenerant flows down like the water, so the bottom of the bed, the last to meet the water, is regenerated worst and some leakage results. In counter-current regeneration the regenerant flows up, so the cleanest resin sits at the outlet; leakage is lower and less regenerant is used.

items: Batch: resin stirred in a tank and filtered off, used for small lots and recovery of a valuable ion.
Fixed bed columns: the usual equipment, pressure vessels with a distributor at the top and a collector under the bed, run in pairs so one serves while the other regenerates.
Two-bed demineraliser: a hydrogen-form cation column turns salts into acids; a degasser strips the CO2 from bicarbonate; a hydroxide-form anion column removes the acids, leaving water.

Mixed bed: cation and anion beads mixed in one vessel act like many two-bed pairs in series and give water of very low conductivity for boilers and electronics; the beads are separated by backwashing for regeneration.
Continuous counter-current units: resin moved in pulses round a loop of service, regeneration and rinse sections, for large steady flows.

blocks.text: Applications go beyond water: recovering chromium and precious metals from plating rinses, extracting uranium from leach liquors, decolourising sugar, purifying antibiotics such as streptomycin, removing radioactive caesium in nuclear plants, and acting as solid acid catalysts.

examples.question: A sodium-form softener treats 500 L/h of water with 4.0 meq/L of hardness (all Ca<sup>2+</sup>) for an 8 h run. The operating capacity is 1.0 eq/L and the bed is regenerated with 150 g NaCl per litre of resin. Find the hardness in mg/L and as CaCO<sub>3</sub>, the resin volume, the salt used per regeneration and the ratio of salt used to the stoichiometric amount.
steps: Hardness: 4.0 meq/L × 20.04 mg/meq (40.08/2) = 80.2 mg/L of Ca<sup>2+</sup>, or 4.0 × 50.04 = 200 mg/L as CaCO<sub>3</sub>.
Equivalents per run = 500 L/h × 8 h × 4.0 meq/L = 16 000 meq = 16 eq. That is 8 mol of Ca<sup>2+</sup> taken up and 16 mol of Na<sup>+</sup> released.
Resin volume = 16 eq/1.0 eq/L = 16 L. (At 1.2 eq/L it would be 13.3 L.)
Salt per regeneration = 150 g/L × 16 L = 2400 g = 2.4 kg.
Stoichiometric salt = 16 eq × 58.44 g/eq = 935 g. Ratio = 2400/935 = 2.57, a regenerant efficiency of 39 %.
examples.answer: 80.2 mg/L Ca<sup>2+</sup> (200 mg/L as CaCO<sub>3</sub>); 16 L of resin; 2.4 kg NaCl per regeneration, 2.57 times the stoichiometric 935 g.

examples.question: A two-bed demineraliser treats 2.0 m³/h of water with 3.0 meq/L of cations and 3.0 meq/L of anions for a 12 h run. Operating capacities are 1.5 eq/L for the cation resin and 1.0 eq/L for the anion resin; each is regenerated with 2.5 times the stoichiometric chemical. Find both resin volumes and the HCl and NaOH per regeneration.
steps: Water per run = 2.0 × 12 = 24 m³ = 24 000 L. Equivalents = 24 000 × 3.0 = 72 000 meq = 72 eq of each sign.
Cation resin = 72/1.5 = 48 L; anion resin = 72/1.0 = 72 L.
examples.answer: 48 L of cation resin and 72 L of anion resin; 6.56 kg HCl and 7.2 kg NaOH per regeneration.

traps: One Ca<sup>2+</sup> releases two Na<sup>+</sup>: the ion count doubles while the equivalents stay equal. Balances are written in equivalents.
Operating capacity, not total capacity, sizes the bed. Using 1.9 eq/L would make the softener too small by half.
Calcium is preferred by the resin, yet brine removes it: high concentration of the regenerant overcomes selectivity.
Ion exchange is a stoichiometric swap of ions throughout the bead, not adsorption of ions on an outer surface.
Hardness as CaCO<sub>3</sub> uses 50.0 mg per meq; as Ca<sup>2+</sup> it uses 20.0 mg per meq. Mixing them gives a factor 2.5 error.

quiz.q: Write the softening reaction on a sodium-form cation resin.
quiz.a: 2R–SO<sub>3</sub>Na + Ca<sup>2+</sup> ⇌ (R–SO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>Ca + 2Na<sup>+</sup>; regeneration with brine drives it to the left.

quiz.q: Why does counter-current regeneration give lower leakage than co-current?
quiz.a: Upflow regenerant meets the outlet end of the bed first, at full strength, so the resin the treated water last touches is the best regenerated. In co-current flow that end gets the weakest regenerant and keeps some hardness, which leaks into the product.

quiz.q: 20 L of resin with an operating capacity of 1.0 eq/L softens 2000 L/h of water with 5 meq/L hardness. Find the run time.
quiz.a: Capacity = 20 eq; load = 2000 × 5 = 10 000 meq/h = 10 eq/h; run = 2.0 h.

quiz.q: Why does a mixed bed give purer water than a two-bed unit?
quiz.a: Each bead pair acts as a cation and anion exchanger in series; with the beads mixed, the water passes through very many such pairs, and the acid formed by one bead is removed at once by the next, so the reaction cannot reverse.

quiz.q: Water holds 120 mg/L of Ca<sup>2+</sup> and 24 mg/L of Mg<sup>2+</sup>. Find the hardness in meq/L and as CaCO<sub>3</sub>.
A strong base anion resin is fed water with chloride, sulfate and bicarbonate. In what order do they break through, and why?
quiz.a: Bicarbonate first, then chloride, then sulfate, since the resin prefers SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> > Cl<sup>−</sup> > HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>; the more strongly held ions displace the weaker ones down the bed and come out last.

beyond: Not for the exam. Electrodeionization fills the cells of an electrodialysis stack with mixed resin and regenerates it continuously with an electric current, so ultrapure water is made without acid and caustic. Chelating resins pick out single metals such as boron or mercury. Search for electrodeionization and chelating resin.

figure.caption: The softener of the worked example. Hard water enters the top of 16 L of sodium-form resin; an exchange zone moves down, leaving calcium-form resin above it, and the water leaves with the same 4.0 meq/L as sodium. After the 8 h run (16 eq) the bed is backwashed, regenerated with 2.4 kg of salt, 2.57 times the stoichiometric 935 g, and rinsed.
